title: The refill decision
bodyMd:
A fictional cooperative offered detergent in disposable bottles and through a refill station. The refill price per litre was lower, but customers first had to buy a durable container. Regular users tended to choose refills; occasional visitors often bought a disposable bottle. The cooperative initially described the latter choice as irrational. A volunteer pointed out that a visitor expecting only one purchase might never recover the container’s initial cost.

The cooperative then introduced a refundable container deposit. Refill use increased among occasional visitors, though some still preferred bottles because the refill station’s opening hours were inconvenient. The experiment suggested that price labels alone did not explain behaviour. Up-front costs, expected future use and the effort of accessing the service all mattered. The organisers continued promoting refills, but began distinguishing a customer’s decision under existing conditions from the conditions they might change.
